name: Creative Commons
tagline: CC empowers individuals and communities around the world through technical, legal, and policy solutions that enable the sharing of education, culture, and science in the public interest.
sdg_alignment: SDG 16 - Peace Justice and Strong Institutions
known_funders: Filecoin Foundation for the Decentralized Web
last_funding_event: 2024 (Open Infrastructure Circle, 20 foundations and companies plus 850 individual donors reported in 2024 Annual Report)
dependency_risks: reliance on voluntary donor renewal for OIC recurring gifts
concentration of anchor funders (5 at $250k+ tier)
legal tool maintenance underfunded relative to adoption scale

news_articles.headline: CC Hosts Open Heritage Statement Event in Amsterdam
AI's Infrastructure Era: Reflections from the AI Impact Summit in Delhi
How to Keep the Internet Human

academic_citations: Broussard (2007). 'The copyleft movement: creative commons licensing.' Communication Research Trends.
Elkin-Koren (2006). 'Exploring Creative Commons: A Skeptical View.' The Future of the Public Domain. Kluwer Law International.

policy_outcomes.description: Fourteen countries adopted national open education policies (as of 2014 State of the Commons report)
Open textbooks using CC licenses saved US students over $100 million (as of 2014 State of the Commons report)
CC licenses adopted by Wikipedia, enabling global free knowledge sharing at scale
CC licenses referenced in EU and national open access mandates for publicly funded research

outcome_methodology: Annual reports and State of the Commons reports quantify adoption metrics (licensed works, geographic reach, institutional adoption) but do not use controlled methodology; policy outcomes documented but causal attribution relies on advocacy accounts.
published_performance_metrics: State of the Commons: ~900M licensed works (2014), ~2B licensed works (2019); 2024 Annual Report: 1,890 CC Certificate graduates across 68 countries
documented_limitations: CC licenses are non-revocable but CC cannot enforce compliance without individual copyright holders acting
No central registry of CC-licensed works — aggregate counts are estimates from platform data
Noncommercial license term ambiguity documented in 2009 'Defining Noncommercial' report
License incompatibility between different CC license variants limits remixing
CC is not a party to any licensing agreement — enforcement responsibility lies with individual rights holders
jurisdictional_scope: international — licenses ported to 75+ jurisdictions; CC 4.0 designed to be jurisdiction-neutral
failure_modes: Large AI companies training on CC-licensed works without attribution or licence compliance
Platform lock-in by commercial intermediaries hosting CC content without preserving license metadata
Funding concentration risk: five anchor funders represent majority of OIC revenue
curation_criteria: CC does not curate licensed works; it maintains the legal and technical infrastructure enabling others to license their own works
contributor_governance: CC Global Network operates via individual membership in national Chapters; board-governed nonprofit; open source projects via GitHub
community_ownership: CC Global Network provides community governance of advocacy and education; legal tools maintained by CC staff and board under 501(c)(3) structure
controversies: Criticism from Richard Stallman/FSF that some CC licenses (NC, ND) do not guarantee software freedoms
Allegations (The Scholarly Kitchen) that CC serves interests of large tech companies including Google
Debian rejected CC Attribution License prior to v3.0 as incompatible with DFSG
Ongoing debate about CC-licensed works used to train AI models without compensation to creators
political_bias_allegations: Allegations that CC disproportionately serves interests of large technology companies (Google, Silicon Valley) at expense of individual creators
legal_regulatory_issues: CC licenses tested in courts in multiple jurisdictions; generally upheld. Ongoing policy engagement on AI training data and copyright.
government_partnerships: Engagement with national governments on open education policy mandates (14 countries as of 2014)
Collaboration with UNESCO on open education resources
ai_involvement: Active policy engagement: published positions on AI training data use of CC-licensed works; developing CC Signals tool for expressing AI-related rights preferences; opposes 'pay-to-crawl' schemes; does not use AI in license tooling
